steps.rendered_prompt:
You are writing a short explainer script from a research record.

Audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy
Target spoken duration: about 60 seconds.

Write the script from the research record below. Make it accurate and easy to follow.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it, in exactly this shape:

{
  "case_id": "C05",
  "audience": "General public with secondary-school science literacy",
  "target_duration_s": 60,
  "beats": [
    {"beat": "short label", "narration": "what the narrator says",
     "on_screen": "what is shown", "claim_refs": []}
  ]
}

RESEARCH RECORD
---------------
A digital CBT app for insomnia: two endpoints, two directions

Record
SYN-C05

Study design
Randomised controlled trial with two pre-registered co-primary endpoints

Background
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the recommended first-line treatment, but access is limited by therapist availability. App-delivered programmes are widely marketed. Trials to date have concentrated on symptom scales; whether symptom change is accompanied by change in daytime function is less well established, which is why both were pre-registered here.

Abstract
We tested a six-week app-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy programme for insomnia against a sleep-hygiene control app. 640 adults with chronic insomnia were randomised 1:1. Two co-primary endpoints were pre-registered: Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) at week 8 and daytime functioning measured by the Work and Social Adjustment Scale (WSAS) at week 8. ISI improved by 6.8 points in the CBT arm versus 3.1 points in control, a between-group difference of 3.7 points (95% CI 2.9 to 4.5, p < 0.001). For WSAS: 1.2 points versus 1.0 points, between-group difference 0.2 points (95% CI -0.7 to 1.1, p = 0.66). Attrition was 14% in the CBT arm and 9% in control. At 6-month follow-up the ISI difference had narrowed to 1.9 points (95% CI 0.6 to 3.2).

Methods
Both endpoints were pre-registered as co-primary and the trial was powered for both. Outcome measures were self-reported. Analysis was intention-to-treat with multiple imputation. Randomisation was 1:1 by an independent service. Participants could not be blinded to app content. The ISI ranges from 0 to 28 and the WSAS from 0 to 40, higher scores worse on both. Six-month follow-up was pre-specified.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis: both co-primary endpoints were tested at a two-sided alpha of 0.025 to preserve the family-wise error rate, and the trial was powered at 90% for each. Missing data were handled by multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption, with a tipping-point sensitivity analysis. Pre-specified subgroup analyses by baseline severity and by age band showed no interaction. Adherence, defined as completing at least four of six modules, was 71% in the CBT arm.

Results
  endpoint: ISI at week 8 (co-primary); cbt: -6.8; control: -3.1; difference: 3.7 (2.9 to 4.5), p<0.001
  endpoint: WSAS daytime functioning at week 8 (co-primary); cbt: -1.2; control: -1.0; difference: 0.2 (-0.7 to 1.1), p=0.66
  endpoint: ISI at 6 months; cbt: -; control: -; difference: 1.9 (0.6 to 3.2)
  endpoint: Attrition; cbt: 14%; control: 9%; difference: -

Discussion
Digital delivery of CBT for insomnia removes the principal access barrier to an effective therapy. The week-8 effect on insomnia severity is comparable to that reported for face-to-face delivery. Attenuation by 6 months is consistent with other digital mental-health interventions and suggests that booster contact may be required. Both pre-registered endpoints are reported in full in the results table.

Limitations
  Self-reported outcomes only; no actigraphy or polysomnography.

Conclusion
App-delivered CBT was compared with a sleep-hygiene control across two pre-registered co-primary endpoints at week 8.

Data availability
De-identified participant data available under a data-sharing agreement.

final_narration:
Talking therapy is the recommended first-line treatment for long-term insomnia. The catch is that there aren't enough therapists to go round. So can an app do the job instead?
Six hundred and forty adults with chronic insomnia were randomly split between a six-week CBT app and a basic sleep-hygiene app. Crucially, the researchers registered two success measures in advance: night-time insomnia symptoms, and how people function in daily life.
On the insomnia symptom scale at week eight, the CBT group improved by 6.8 points, against 3.1 in the control group. That's a 3.7-point advantage, and the result is unlikely to be chance.
But on the second measure, how well people managed work and social life, the two apps were indistinguishable. Just 0.2 points apart, and the range of plausible values includes no benefit at all.
The sleep benefit also faded: by six months the gap had narrowed to 1.9 points. And everything here was self-reported, with no sleep-lab measurements. So the honest summary is this: the app eased insomnia symptoms, but it has yet to show that it changes people's days.
